speaker: ALEX
text: Episode 18 is the glossary. Today we are turning Git, GitHub, open source, and accessibility terms into something you can actually use.

speaker: JAMIE
text: I am listening for the plain-English version: what the word means, when it shows up, and what a learner should do next.

speaker: ALEX
text: That is the promise of this glossary. Not just definitions, but useful moves. By the end, the terms should feel like tools, not noise.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the job is to make the vocabulary teachable, not just searchable.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Think of this as a map for the whole workshop: when you hear a term you do not know, you can pause, find it, and keep going.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Start us at the beginning.

speaker: ALEX
text: Every Term You Need for Open Source Contribution. That is the big idea. When you run into a word you have not seen before, check the glossary first.

speaker: ALEX
text: And the learning cards are there to help you navigate it. They do three things: name the term, give you a practical move, and show what evidence to look for.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What should a learner use to get around the glossary?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use headings to jump between sections, use the Elements List in a screen reader to browse terms, and use the alphabetical quick reference when you want a fast lookup. If you are zoomed in, the short heading list and the A-to-Z table are both helpful.

speaker: ALEX
text: Part 1 is the building blocks.

speaker: ALEX
text: Repository, or repo, is the container for a project. It holds the files, folders, history, and everything Git knows about the work.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That one matters because it is where the whole story lives.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. Organization, or org, is a GitHub group account. Teams often place open source projects there instead of under a personal account.

speaker: ALEX
text: A fork is your own copy of someone else's repository in your GitHub account. Pronunciation note: fork means the copy of the repo, not a literal fork in a road.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So if I fork a project, I get my own version to work from.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Remote means a repository hosted somewhere else, usually on GitHub. Your local repo can point to more than one remote.

speaker: ALEX
text: If you want to see your remotes, a common command is `git remote -v`. If you want to add one, you might use `git remote add upstream <url>`. Read commands as examples first, not as magic words.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And origin?

speaker: ALEX
text: Origin is the default name Git gives to the remote you cloned from. Most of the time, origin points to your fork. Upstream is the original project you forked from.

speaker: ALEX
text: `.gitignore` is a file in the root of the repo that tells Git what not to track. Use it for build files, temporary files, secret files, and editor-specific clutter.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So it helps keep the repository clean.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Example entries might include `dist/`, `node_modules/`, `.env`, `.vscode/`, or `.idea/`. Important detail: `.gitignore` only affects files Git has not already started tracking.

speaker: ALEX
text: Clone means copying a repository from GitHub down to your computer so you can work on it locally.

speaker: ALEX
text: Branch is a separate line of development inside a repository. Most work happens on branches, not directly on the stable main line.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What are the common branch names people should recognize?

speaker: ALEX
text: `main` is usually the primary branch. `develop` is sometimes used as an integration branch. `feature/my-change` is a common feature branch pattern. `fix/button-label` is a common bugfix pattern. `docs/update-readme` is for documentation work.

speaker: ALEX
text: Commit is a saved snapshot of your changes at a moment in time. A good commit message says what changed, not just that something changed.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And the diff?

speaker: ALEX
text: A diff shows the difference between two versions of a file. Added lines usually show up as green or with a plus sign. Deleted lines show the opposite.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Move into collaboration.

speaker: ALEX
text: Issue is a discussion item in a GitHub repository. People use issues for bugs, features, questions, and ideas. It usually has a number, a title, a body, labels, comments, and sometimes assignees or milestones.

speaker: ALEX
text: Pull request, or PR, is a proposal to merge changes from one branch into another. You use it to say, "Here is the work, please review it."

speaker: JAMIE
text: That is the handoff point.

speaker: ALEX
text: Code review is when collaborators read the pull request and give feedback before merge. Good reviews are specific, kind, and useful.

speaker: ALEX
text: Merge is combining changes from one branch into another. When a PR is approved, someone with permission or responsibility may merge it.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What about the nasty case?

speaker: ALEX
text: Merge conflict happens when two branches change the same part of the same file in incompatible ways. Git stops and asks a human to decide.

speaker: ALEX
text: Upstream, in collaboration language, is the original repository a fork came from. When the original project changes, you may sync your fork with upstream.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And labels, milestones, and projects?

speaker: ALEX
text: Label is a tag you add to an issue or PR to categorize it. Milestone groups work toward a shared target. Project, in GitHub Projects, is a planning board for organizing work across issues and PRs.

speaker: ALEX
text: Part 3 is people and roles.

speaker: ALEX
text: Maintainer is the person or team that keeps the project healthy and makes final calls.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Contributor is the person doing the work.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Contributor is anyone who adds code, docs, tests, or fixes.

speaker: ALEX
text: Triage is the process of sorting and prioritizing incoming issues or PRs. Collaborator is someone with permission to help manage the repository.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What about the shorthand people hear in chats and docs?

speaker: ALEX
text: That is Part 4: common abbreviations and slang. Repo means repository. Org means organization. PR means pull request. CI means continuous integration. CD often means continuous delivery or continuous deployment. Dev usually means developer or development. SHA is the commit hash, like a fingerprint. Pronunciation note: SHA is usually said "sha," and CI/CD is often said as separate letters.

speaker: ALEX
text: Part 5 is the technical GitHub concepts.

speaker: ALEX
text: HEAD is the commit or branch you are currently on. It is where Git says, "this is the point I'm looking at right now."

speaker: JAMIE
text: Detached HEAD sounds scary.

speaker: ALEX
text: Detached HEAD means HEAD points to a commit instead of a branch. It can happen when you check out a specific commit or tag. It is not a disaster, but it means new commits are not attached to a named branch unless you create one.

speaker: ALEX
text: Stash is a temporary place to save unfinished changes so you can switch tasks without committing them.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What is the usual stash workflow?

speaker: ALEX
text: Save the work, switch branches, do the urgent task, then bring the stash back later. You might hear commands like `git stash`, `git stash list`, and `git stash pop`.

speaker: ALEX
text: Rebase is a way to move or replay commits onto a different base commit. Merge and rebase can both combine work, but they do it differently.

speaker: JAMIE
text: When should someone use rebase?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use rebase when you want a cleaner linear history and you understand the branch is yours or the team agrees on that workflow. Do not rebase shared history casually.

speaker: ALEX
text: Cherry-pick means taking one specific commit and applying it somewhere else. It is useful when you want a single fix without the rest of the branch.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And fetch versus pull?

speaker: ALEX
text: Fetch downloads new information from a remote without changing your working branch. Pull does a fetch and then brings those changes into your branch.

speaker: ALEX
text: Force push is pushing changes in a way that overwrites remote history. It can be necessary after a rebase, but it is risky.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So when is it okay?

speaker: ALEX
text: Only when you know the impact and your team expects it. Never use force push on shared work unless that is part of the plan. A safer option is `--force-with-lease`.

speaker: ALEX
text: SHA or hash is the unique identifier for a commit. It looks like a long string of letters and numbers, and GitHub often shows a shorter version in the UI.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Now bring it back to GitHub workflow terms.

speaker: ALEX
text: A review can be draft, meaning it is still a work in progress. Status checks are automated results from tests or workflows that must pass before merge in many projects.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So a PR is not just code, it is a conversation plus evidence.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. And the workflow terms fit together: branch, commit, push, pull, clone, fork, issue, PR, review, merge conflict, status check, merge.

speaker: ALEX
text: Now the accessibility terms.

speaker: ALEX
text: Screen reader is software that reads page content aloud or sends it to a Braille display. It helps blind and low-vision users navigate content.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What is a landmark?

speaker: ALEX
text: A landmark is a major page region, like navigation, main content, or search. Landmarks help screen reader users jump around efficiently.

speaker: ALEX
text: A heading gives structure to the page. It lets people scan, jump, and understand the hierarchy of content.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And ARIA?

speaker: ALEX
text: ARIA stands for Accessible Rich Internet Applications. It adds accessibility information when native HTML is not enough, but it should be used carefully and only when needed.

speaker: ALEX
text: Focus is where keyboard interaction currently lives. Tab order is the sequence focus moves through the page when someone presses Tab.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So if tab order is broken, keyboard users feel it immediately.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. That is why logical focus order matters so much.

speaker: ALEX
text: Now the agent terms.

speaker: ALEX
text: Copilot is GitHub's AI assistant. It can help draft code, docs, commit messages, and other text.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And an agent?

speaker: ALEX
text: An agent is a more autonomous assistant that can take actions on your behalf inside a workflow.

speaker: ALEX
text: A slash command is a typed command that starts with `/`, usually inside a chat or agent interface. It triggers a specific action.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So a prompt is the instruction you give the model.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. And an instruction file is a file that stores guidance for the agent or assistant so it can follow consistent project rules.

speaker: ALEX
text: A few pronunciation notes help too. Repo is short for repository. Org is short for organization. PR is said "pee-arr." ARIA is usually said "air-ee-uh." SHA is said "sha." Git is "git," not "jift."

speaker: JAMIE
text: That kind of detail removes a lot of friction.

speaker: ALEX
text: It does. The point of the glossary is not to impress anyone. It is to lower the barrier between hearing a term and knowing what to do.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So what should people carry forward?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use the glossary like a working map. Repository, branch, commit, diff, issue, pull request, review, merge conflict, status check, upstream, remote, local, screen reader, landmark, heading, ARIA, focus, tab order, Copilot, agent, slash command, prompt, instruction file.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That is the list that turns the episode into a reference.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. If the term is unclear, pause, look it up, and continue with confidence. That is episode 18.
